units.title: Motion in One Dimension
units.blurb: Describe motion along a line with signs, graphs and the constant-acceleration equations.

units.title: Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions
units.blurb: Split vectors into components, add them, change reference frames and follow projectiles.

units.title: Forces and Newton's Laws
units.blurb: Draw free-body diagrams and use Newton's laws with friction, ropes, springs, gravity and circles.

units.title: Work, Energy and Power
units.blurb: Follow energy as forces do work on a system, with bar charts and conservation.

units.title: Momentum
units.blurb: Use impulse and the conservation of momentum to analyze collisions and explosions.

units.title: Torque and Rotational Dynamics
units.blurb: Describe turning with angles, find torques, and use the rotational form of Newton's laws.

units.title: Energy and Momentum of Rotating Systems
units.blurb: Spinning objects store energy and carry angular momentum, which is conserved without outside torques.

units.title: Oscillations
units.blurb: Restoring forces make motion repeat; find periods, energies and the graphs of simple harmonic motion.

topics.title: Checking Equations with Units
topics.short: Every term in a physics equation must have the same units, which catches many mistakes before they happen.
topics.trouble: Students add quantities with different units, or keep an answer whose units show the formula was misremembered.

topics.title: Position and Displacement on an Axis
topics.short: Pick an origin and a positive direction; displacement Δx = x_final − x_initial carries a sign.
topics.trouble: Students compute displacement as the total distance traveled, ignoring a change of direction.

topics.title: Average Velocity
topics.short: Average velocity is Δx/Δt, with a sign; average speed uses total distance instead.
topics.trouble: Students find average velocity by averaging the starting and ending speeds even when the acceleration changes.

topics.title: Position-Time Graphs
topics.short: The slope of an x–t graph is the velocity.
topics.trouble: Students read a high point on the graph as a high speed, mixing up the value with the slope.

topics.title: Instantaneous Velocity
topics.short: The velocity at an instant is the slope of the tangent line to the x–t graph.
topics.trouble: Students think an object at x = 0 must have zero velocity, mixing up position with velocity.

topics.title: Acceleration and Its Sign
topics.short: a = Δv/Δt; an object slows down when its acceleration points opposite to its velocity.
topics.trouble: Students think negative acceleration always means slowing down.

topics.title: Velocity-Time Graphs
topics.short: On a v–t graph the slope is the acceleration and the area under the line is the displacement.
topics.trouble: Students read a v–t graph as if it showed position, thinking a downward slope means moving backward.

topics.title: Translating Between Motion Graphs
topics.short: Turn an x–t graph into v–t and a–t graphs, and back again.
topics.trouble: Students copy the shape of one graph onto the next instead of tracking slopes.

topics.title: The Constant-Acceleration Equations
topics.short: v = v₀ + at and x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² hold when the acceleration is constant.
topics.trouble: Students use these equations even when the acceleration changes partway through the motion.

topics.title: Motion Without the Time
topics.short: v² = v₀² + 2aΔx links speeds and displacement when the time isn't known.
topics.trouble: Students forget the 2, or take a square root and lose the velocity's direction.

topics.title: Free Fall
topics.short: Without air resistance, every dropped object speeds up by 9.8 m/s each second, whatever its mass.
topics.trouble: Students think heavier objects fall faster.

topics.title: Thrown Straight Up
topics.short: Going up, at the top and coming down, the acceleration is the same 9.8 m/s² downward.
topics.trouble: Students think the acceleration is zero at the top, where the velocity is zero for an instant.

topics.title: Vectors and Their Components
topics.short: Split a vector into x- and y-components with sine and cosine.
topics.trouble: Students use sine for the x-component every time, instead of checking which side is next to the angle.

topics.title: Adding Vectors by Components
topics.short: Add the x-parts and the y-parts, then find the size and direction of the result.
topics.trouble: Students add magnitudes directly, so 3 N and 4 N at right angles give 7 N instead of 5 N.

topics.title: Relative Velocity
topics.short: Velocities add as vectors when you change reference frames: boats in rivers, planes in wind.
topics.trouble: Students add the river's speed to the boat's speed when the boat heads straight across.

topics.title: Launched Horizontally
topics.short: Horizontal motion stays steady while vertical motion is free fall, and both share the same time.
topics.trouble: Students think a ball fired horizontally lands later than one dropped from the same height.

topics.title: Launched at an Angle
topics.short: Split the launch velocity into parts, treat each direction on its own, and use the symmetry of the path.
topics.trouble: Students think the velocity is zero at the top of the path, forgetting the horizontal part.

topics.title: Systems and Center of Mass
topics.short: Choose what is in your system; its center of mass is the mass-weighted average position.
topics.trouble: Students put the center of mass halfway between two objects whatever their masses.

topics.title: Free-Body Diagrams
topics.short: Draw every force on one object as an arrow from its center, naming what exerts it.
topics.trouble: Students draw a "force of motion" in the direction an object moves, or include forces the object exerts on other things.

topics.title: Newton's Third Law Pairs
topics.short: The two forces of a pair act on different objects, are the same type and are equal in size.
topics.trouble: Students call weight and the normal force a third-law pair, or think the heavier object pushes harder.

topics.title: Equilibrium and the First Law
topics.short: Zero net force means constant velocity, and standing still is the special case where that velocity is zero.
topics.trouble: Students think an object moving at constant speed needs a net force in its direction of motion.

topics.title: Newton's Second Law Along an Axis
topics.short: Add the forces along an axis with signs, then a = ΣF/m.
topics.trouble: Students use only the applied force instead of the net force.

topics.title: The Normal Force and Apparent Weight
topics.short: A surface pushes as hard as it must; in an accelerating elevator the scale reading differs from mg.
topics.trouble: Students assume the normal force always equals mg.

topics.title: Forces at Angles
topics.short: Resolve each force into components; the x and y directions each obey Newton's second law separately.
topics.trouble: Students forget that a rope pulling up at an angle also lowers the normal force.

topics.title: Inclined Planes
topics.short: On a ramp at angle θ, gravity splits into mg sin θ along the slope and mg cos θ into it.
topics.trouble: Students swap sine and cosine for the two parts of the weight on a slope.

topics.title: Kinetic Friction
topics.short: A sliding object feels friction f_k = μ_k N against its sliding.
topics.trouble: Students use mg instead of the normal force when the normal force isn't mg.

topics.title: Static Friction
topics.short: Static friction matches the push up to a limit of μ_s N; beyond that, the object slides.
topics.trouble: Students always set static friction equal to μ_s N, even when the object is far from slipping.

topics.title: Friction on Ramps
topics.short: Find the angle where a block starts to slip, tan θ = μ_s, and its acceleration once it slides.
topics.trouble: Students point friction down the slope for a block that is sliding down.

topics.title: Connected Objects and Tension
topics.short: Treat linked objects as one system to find a, then one object alone to find the tension.
topics.trouble: Students think the rope's tension equals the applied force or the hanging weight.

topics.title: Pulleys and the Atwood Machine
topics.short: A light rope over a light pulley has one tension, and the whole system speeds up together.
topics.trouble: Students set the tension equal to the hanging mass's weight even while it accelerates.

topics.title: Spring Forces and Hooke's Law
topics.short: A stretched or squeezed spring pushes back with F = kx, in proportion to how far it is stretched or squeezed.
topics.trouble: Students use the spring's total length instead of its stretch from its natural length.

topics.title: Newton's Law of Gravitation
topics.short: F = Gm₁m₂/r², with r measured between the centers.
topics.trouble: Students measure r from a planet's surface instead of its center.

topics.title: Gravitational Field Strength
topics.short: g = GM/r² is the gravitational force on each kilogram near a planet.
topics.trouble: Students think g is zero in orbit, or the same at every height.

topics.title: Centripetal Acceleration
topics.short: Moving in a circle at steady speed means accelerating toward the center: a = v²/r.
topics.trouble: Students think an object moving at a constant speed can't be accelerating.

topics.title: Forces in Circular Motion
topics.short: A real force such as tension, friction or gravity supplies the net inward force mv²/r.
topics.trouble: Students add an outward "centrifugal force" to the free-body diagram, or think a released ball flies straight outward.

topics.title: Vertical Circles
topics.short: At the top and bottom of a loop or a dip, the net force toward the center is mv²/r.
topics.trouble: Students think the normal force at the bottom of a dip equals mg.

topics.title: Work by a Constant Force
topics.short: W = Fd cos θ, and a force at right angles to the motion does no work.
topics.trouble: Students think every force on a moving object does work, including the normal force on a level road.

topics.title: Work as Area Under a Force Graph
topics.short: The area under a force–position graph is the work done.
topics.trouble: Students multiply the final force by the distance when the force changes along the way.

topics.title: The Work-Energy Theorem
topics.short: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.
topics.trouble: Students use the work of one force instead of the work of the net force.

topics.title: Gravitational Potential Energy of a System
topics.short: ΔU = mgΔh belongs to the Earth–object system, and only changes in it matter.
topics.trouble: Students think the potential energy depends on the path taken between two heights.

topics.title: Elastic Potential Energy
topics.short: A spring stretched or squeezed by x stores ½kx².
topics.trouble: Students write kx² without the ½, or use the force kx as if it were energy.

topics.title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
topics.short: When only gravity and springs do work, K + U stays the same.
topics.trouble: Students think a heavier object reaches the bottom of a frictionless ramp with a higher speed.

topics.title: Energy Bar Charts
topics.short: Show the energy at the start, the energy that crosses the system boundary, and the energy at the end.
topics.trouble: Students leave out the energy that enters or leaves the system as work.

topics.title: Friction and Thermal Energy
topics.short: Friction turns mechanical energy into thermal energy: ΔE_thermal = f_k d.
topics.trouble: Students think energy disappears when friction stops a sliding box.

topics.title: Power
topics.short: Power is the rate of energy transfer: P = W/Δt = Fv.
topics.trouble: Students mix up power with energy, or use P = Fv with a force that isn't along the velocity.

topics.title: Gravitational Potential Energy Far from Earth
topics.short: U = −Gm₁m₂/r, which is zero when the objects are infinitely far apart.
topics.trouble: Students are puzzled that the energy is negative, or use mgh for heights comparable to Earth's radius.

topics.title: Linear Momentum
topics.short: Momentum p = mv is a vector, and a system's momentum is the vector sum of its parts.
topics.trouble: Students add momenta as plain numbers, forgetting that opposite directions cancel.

topics.title: Impulse and Change in Momentum
topics.short: FΔt = Δp, and the area under a force–time graph is the impulse.
topics.trouble: Students think a ball that bounces back has a smaller change in momentum than one that stops dead.

topics.title: Conservation of Momentum
topics.short: With no net outside force, the total momentum of a system stays the same.
topics.trouble: Students think momentum is conserved only in bouncy, elastic collisions.

topics.title: Sticking Collisions
topics.short: Objects that stick move off together: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v.
topics.trouble: Students conserve kinetic energy in a collision where the objects stick together.

topics.title: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions
topics.short: Kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions; compare K before and after to classify one.
topics.trouble: Students think kinetic energy, like momentum, is always conserved.

topics.title: Explosions and Recoil
topics.short: Pieces that start at rest fly apart with equal and opposite momenta.
topics.trouble: Students think the lighter piece gets more momentum because it moves faster.

topics.title: Motion of the Center of Mass
topics.short: With no outside force, a system's center of mass keeps moving at a steady velocity.
topics.trouble: Students think an explosion changes the path of the center of mass.

topics.title: Angle, Angular Velocity and Angular Acceleration
topics.short: Measure turning in radians: ω = Δθ/Δt and α = Δω/Δt.
topics.trouble: Students mix degrees, revolutions and radians in one calculation.

topics.title: Rotational Kinematics
topics.short: ω = ω₀ + αt and θ = ω₀t + ½αt² mirror the straight-line equations.
topics.trouble: Students put a distance where the angle belongs, or mix revolutions with radians.

topics.title: Linking Linear and Rotational Motion
topics.short: A point at radius r moves with v = rω and tangential acceleration a = rα.
topics.trouble: Students think every point on a spinning wheel moves at the same speed.

topics.title: Torque
topics.short: Torque is a force times its lever arm: τ = rF sin θ.
topics.trouble: Students think a bigger force always makes a bigger torque, whatever its direction and where it acts.

topics.title: Rotational Equilibrium
topics.short: A balanced object has zero net force and zero net torque about any point you choose.
topics.trouble: Students think the choice of pivot point changes the answer, or leave out the force acting at the pivot.

topics.title: Rotational Inertia
topics.short: I = Σmr²: mass far from the axis makes an object harder to spin.
topics.trouble: Students think rotational inertia depends only on the mass, not on how far the mass is from the axis.

topics.title: Newton's Second Law for Rotation
topics.short: The net torque equals Iα.
topics.trouble: Students use the force instead of the torque, or the mass instead of the rotational inertia.

topics.title: Pulleys with Mass
topics.short: Solve a hanging mass on a heavy pulley with τ = Iα and F = ma together.
topics.trouble: Students assume the rope's tension is the same on both sides of a pulley that has mass.

topics.title: Rotational Kinetic Energy and Work by Torque
topics.short: A spinning object stores ½Iω², and a torque turning it through Δθ does work τΔθ.
topics.trouble: Students use ½mv² with the rim speed for an object that only spins.

topics.title: Rolling Without Slipping
topics.short: A rolling object shares its energy between moving and spinning, so a hoop rolls down a ramp more slowly than a ball.
topics.trouble: Students think the heavier or larger ball wins a rolling race.

topics.title: Angular Momentum and Angular Impulse
topics.short: L = Iω for a spinning object and L = mvr⊥ for a passing point mass; a torque acting for a time changes L by τΔt.
topics.trouble: Students think an object moving in a straight line can't have angular momentum.

topics.title: Conservation of Angular Momentum
topics.short: With no outside torque Iω stays the same, so a skater who pulls in her arms spins faster.
topics.trouble: Students think the skater's kinetic energy stays the same when she pulls her arms in; it grows, because she does work.

topics.title: Satellites in Orbit
topics.short: Gravity supplies the centripetal force, so v = √(GM/r) and lower orbits are faster.
topics.trouble: Students think astronauts float because there is no gravity in orbit, when they and their ship are falling together.

topics.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.short: A restoring force proportional to displacement makes motion repeat with a fixed amplitude, period and frequency.
topics.trouble: Students think the acceleration is greatest at the middle, where the speed is greatest.

topics.title: Period of a Mass on a Spring
topics.short: T = 2π√(m/k), whatever the amplitude.
topics.trouble: Students think a bigger amplitude makes the period longer.

topics.title: Period of a Pendulum
topics.short: For small swings T = 2π√(L/g), and the mass of the bob doesn't matter.
topics.trouble: Students think a heavier bob swings more slowly.

topics.title: Energy in Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.short: Energy swaps between ½kx² and ½mv², and the total is ½kA².
topics.trouble: Students think the speed is greatest at the turning points.

topics.title: Graphs of Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.short: Position, velocity and acceleration follow sine and cosine curves, each a quarter cycle apart.
topics.trouble: Students think position and velocity reach their peaks at the same moment.
